item.title: The Relationship Skill Nobody Teaches
item.description:
Relationships

The Relationship Skill Nobody Teaches

Repair may matter more than avoiding conflict.

Posted June 24, 2026

Key points
  • Small ruptures often have a greater impact than we realise when they go unaddressed.
  • Healthy relationships are strengthened through repair, not by avoiding honesty.
  • Repair does not require agreement; it requires humility and a genuine interest in the other’s experience.
  • Teams become more resilient when they learn how to find their way back to one another.
Repair is an expression of commitment
Source: Franckreporter / iStock

A few years ago, I witnessed a disagreement between two highly respected colleagues. It was not dramatic by any objective measure. No voices were raised, no accusations were made, and if you had walked into the room halfway through the conversation, you might not have noticed anything unusual at all. Yet afterwards, something had clearly changed.

The ease that had characterised their interactions seemed absent. Meetings became more formal, conversations shortened, and there was a subtle distance where there had once been warmth. No rupture had been openly acknowledged, and perhaps that was part of the problem.

Many of us assume that successful relationships are those where conflict rarely occurs. We imagine that strong teams, nourishing partnerships, and healthy workplaces are somehow free from misunderstanding or tension. Yet the longer I have worked in healthcare, the less convincing that idea has become.

Wherever human beings work closely together, there will be moments of disappointment, friction, miscommunication, and hurt. People become tired, pressure increases, and assumptions are made. A comment lands differently than intended, and maybe someone feels overlooked, criticised, or misunderstood.

What interests me is not whether these moments occur, but what happens afterwards.

Researcher John Gottman, whose work has shaped our understanding of long-term relationships, found that conflict itself is often less important than the ability to repair after rupture. The relationships that endure are not necessarily those with the fewest disagreements. They are the ones in which people find ways to reconnect after periods of disconnection.

Although John Gottman's research focused primarily on couples, the principle feels equally relevant in healthcare teams, organisations, and leadership environments. We spend considerable time learning how to communicate. We learn how to give feedback, navigate difficult conversations, and collaborate effectively. Very little attention is given to what happens when communication breaks down, trust is strained, or relationships become unsettled, and yet these moments are inevitable.

One reason repair can feel so difficult is that relational tension often activates our protective instincts. We may defend our position, withdraw from the conversation, suppress what we are really feeling, or minimise the significance of what happened altogether. Although these responses are understandable, they often deepen the distance between people rather than restore connection. Curiosity narrows; listening becomes harder, and the relationship itself can quietly disappear from view.

Most repairs begin in surprisingly ordinary ways. Someone checks in after a difficult meeting. A colleague acknowledges that a comment landed differently than intended. A leader circles back to a conversation that did not sit comfortably. A team member asks a simple question: "Can we talk about what happened?"

What matters is less the specific form it takes than the willingness to move towards the relationship rather than away from it.

At its heart, repair is an expression of commitment. It reflects a decision that the relationship matters more than the temporary discomfort of addressing what has gone wrong. Importantly, repair does not require agreement. Nor does it require someone to abandon their perspective or accept blame for everything that occurred. Often it begins with a genuine effort to understand another person's experience, even when our own intentions were entirely reasonable.

Trust tends to grow in environments where people know that difficulties can be addressed openly, where misunderstandings do not have to be hidden, and where mistakes become opportunities for learning rather than sources of shame. This is part of what psychological safety really means in practice. It is less about comfort than confidence: confidence that the relationship can withstand honesty.

This may help explain why some teams remain remarkably resilient despite significant pressures. They are not protected from conflict; they simply develop the capacity to repair more quickly when conflict arises. Small moments matter here. A brief conversation after a misunderstanding. A sincere apology, or a willingness to revisit an uncomfortable interaction rather than pretend it never happened. Such gestures may seem insignificant, yet they often prevent small ruptures from becoming lasting divisions.

The healthiest teams I have encountered are rarely the ones in which everything runs smoothly. More often, they are the ones in which people have developed enough trust to address difficulties before they become divisions and enough humility to find their way back to one another when they drift apart.

The longer I work in healthcare, the more I suspect that repair is one of the most underrated relational skills we possess. It strengthens trust, it deepens understanding, and it allows relationships to recover from the ordinary imperfections of being human.

Perhaps this is part of what compassionate leadership really asks of us. Not perfection and certainly not endless agreement. Just the courage to remain in a relationship when things become difficult and the wisdom to recognise that some of our strongest connections are forged not through avoiding rupture but through finding our way back from it.

The capacity to repair may also be one of the foundations upon which trust, belonging, authenticity, and psychological safety are built. Before people can feel fully seen, fully heard, or fully valued, they need confidence that relationships can survive moments of strain. Repair creates that confidence.

item.title: The Trauma of Repeated Hope in Infertility
item.description:
Infertility

The Trauma of Repeated Hope in Infertility

When hoping becomes something the body learns to fear.

Posted June 24, 2026

Key points
  • Repeated cycles can condition the brain to fear hope itself, not just in anticipation of loss.
  • Grief in IVF is not a single event. It is cyclical, procedural, and present at every stage of treatment.
  • Each new cycle begins before the grief from the last one has been processed.
  • Shifting from "what if" to "even if" offers a way to hold hope that is grounded rather than depleting.
Repeated Cycles And Loss
Source: Vadymvdrobot/Envato

What happens when the thing keeping you going becomes the thing you're most afraid of?

For many people in fertility treatment, hope is the answer to that question.

If you have been through multiple cycles of fertility treatment, you may have noticed something shift. At some point, hope stopped feeling like an anchor and started feeling like a threat.

Understanding why that happens requires looking at what infertility actually does to the nervous system over time.

How Infertility Differs From Other Losses

Loss is one of the main pain points in fertility counselling. After so many cycles of hoping and not getting there, hope can start to feel dangerous.

What makes this more than emotional exhaustion is the effect it has on the nervous system over time.

Trauma is not defined by the size of a single event. It is defined by what happens inside the nervous system when an experience overwhelms its capacity to cope and integrate. By that definition, repeated infertility loss can qualify.

Unlike a single traumatic event, infertility rarely involves one defining moment of loss. Instead, it involves a recurring cycle: anticipation, optimism, uncertainty, and devastation, repeated month after month, cycle after cycle. Each embryo transfer, pregnancy test, and menstrual cycle invites hope. And each one risks another emotional wound.

Qualitative research based on clinical psychotherapy with involuntarily childless women suggests that infertility does not just cause emotional distress. It can erode a person's fundamental sense of who they are (Archetti, 2024).

This is what makes infertility psychologically distinct. The grief is ongoing, and the outcome remains uncertain. Together, they keep the wound open.

And hope, the very thing that makes continuing possible, is also the thing that keeps reopening the wound.

What the Brain Learns

The brain is wired for one thing above everything else: survival.

A key part of that system is the amygdala, the brain’s threat detection center, which constantly scans for patterns that predict danger. When a stimulus is repeatedly followed by pain, the amygdala encodes it as a threat cue. The brain learns to activate a defensive response when that signal appears.

This is classical fear conditioning. In the context of repeated fertility treatment, hope becomes that signal.

The brain is also built for efficiency.

Rather than processing each new experience from scratch, it takes shortcuts, using past experience to predict what comes next and conserve mental energy.

This is predictive coding. The brain builds an internal model of what to expect, based on what it has already lived through, and defaults to that model to save energy (Ali et al., 2022).

After enough cycles of hoping and losing, the brain stops waiting for the results. Then, based on everything it has learned, it starts guessing a loss.

This is why, by the third or fourth cycle, something has already changed. In the beginning, hope felt automatic. By cycle four, it feels like something to brace against.

Research documents this pattern: women undergoing repeated IVF cycles gradually withdraw emotionally, pulling away from hope not by choice, but as a protective response (Ying et al., 2024). They begin expecting the worst because the brain has learned that expecting the worst is the only available protection.

There is a painful internal logic to it. Without hope, you cannot be disappointed. If you do not allow yourself to imagine the future, losing it hurts less. The emotional numbness that sets in is a conditioned fear response.

The nervous system contracts around a stimulus it has learned to dread.

Why the Brain Cannot Recover Between Cycles

What makes this pattern specifically traumatic is not only that the brain learns to fear hope. It is the structure of fertility treatments that keeps the nervous system from completing its own recovery.

In typical fear conditioning, recovery is possible. Given time and the absence of the threatening pattern, the brain can learn that the feared stimulus no longer predicts danger. It can process what happened, integrate the experience, and recalibrate.

Fertility treatment does not allow for this.

Before one loss has been fully processed, the next cycle begins. Hope is reactivated before grief has anywhere to go.

A 2025 study published in Scientific Reports found that grief in the context of IVF is not a single event but a cyclical, procedural, ongoing emotional experience, with loss present at every stage of treatment (Gershfeld-Litvin et al., 2025).

The grief does not wait for the result. It is already there, at every stage, and it never gets to finish.

Patients describe suppressing grief and setting it aside because there is another cycle to prepare for. Another round of injections, another retrieval, another two-week wait. Grief gets filed away because the treatment calendar does not pause for it.

Over time, this creates something heavier than sadness: the accumulated weight of multiple losses that were never allowed to finish, stacked beneath a surface that has to keep functioning.

The nervous system is simultaneously conditioned to fear and hope, while being denied the recovery process that could interrupt that conditioning.

That is the mechanism by which repeated hope in infertility becomes traumatic.

From "What If" to "Even If": Cultivating Grounded Hope

Grounded Hope
Source: Stepan Popov/Envato

Repeated losses shatter hope. But the goal is not to rebuild the same kind of hope that broke. It is to develop something more durable: grounded hope.

Ungrounded hope says, "What if?"

What if this cycle works? What if this time is different? It is fragile because it falls on a single outcome. When that outcome does not come, the brain files it away as confirmation of what it has already learned. Hope hurts.

Grounded hope says, "Even if."

Even if this cycle does not work, I will find a way through. Even if the answer is not what I want, I will figure out what comes next. This is hope that can hold both possibility and uncertainty at the same time, without being destroyed by either.

Grounded hope is built slowly, through repeated small acts of tolerating uncertainty rather than bracing against it.

But it is a different relationship with hope, one that the nervous system can sustain.

item.title: When Priorities Compete, How Do You Choose?
item.description:
Traumatic Brain Injury

When Priorities Compete, How Do You Choose?

Personal Perspective: Lessons in deciding between competing priorities.

Posted June 24, 2026

Source: Gerd Altmann/Pixabay

When you suffer a brain injury, your life turns into competing top priorities. I was asked to write on the following question: When everything is a high priority, how do you decide which one to tackle?

Catastrophic brain injury can affect every part of your life and every part of you, giving rise to multiple top priorities, which leads to things going awry financially, socially, in family relationships, health and health care, psychologically, cognitively, emotionally, concerning shelter, activities of daily living, and so on.

The first step to corralling order is deciding which is the most important to you, then making that an absolute, immovable topmost priority in every decision.

If you let other priorities take precedence, then either it isn’t as important as you thought, or you’re letting other people or other priorities dictate your topmost priority. If it’s the former, re-evaluate. If it’s the latter, stick notes on your fridge, your bathroom mirror, computer, and anywhere else to remind you that this area is topmost in every priority decision.

For me, it’s health.

Without health, all else worsens.

For a person with a brain injury, survival isn’t only about food, shelter, and clothing; it’s also about healing the injury.

Unfortunately, Canada's Medicare doesn't cover restorative neurostimulation and neuromodulation treatments. Private insurance for psychological, chiropractic, and/or physiotherapy may cover all or part of it. In the US, the situation may be similar. And so at first glance, these treatments that radically heal the brain appear unaffordable.

I faced this conundrum when I first found brain biofeedback at the ADD Centre. I needed it to restore my concentration, but I had no income and was mired in insurance lawsuits. I faced two competing priorities: health versus finances.

But I’d made health my topmost priority, which included restoring all my cognitive functioning. That meant I had to make the finances work, not elevate finances above my health. Where you put your focus, as well as having financial management skills, determines how much you can achieve.

For this reason, many have called for high schools to teach financial literacy; for example, Ontario will require financial literacy graduation to earn a high school diploma.

My mother began teaching me financial literacy when I was 8 years old; my parents’ accountant taught me basic small-business accounting. I adopted financial software early on. And so, even though confabulation tanked my credit rating by misleading me into thinking I’d paid my bills, I had enough of those skills left to know how to budget, the order of loans versus using savings, and how to negotiate in good humour with good faith when devising a way to afford neurostimulation.

My plan boiled down to: I need brain biofeedback; where can I take the money from; and can I reduce the monthly cost?

But if you didn’t develop or retain financial literacy, then either rely on a trustworthy person to make a plan or make finances your topmost priority so that you don’t end up in ever-increasing debt. The downside is that finances as the topmost priority may mean not being able to access neurostimulation and being stuck with the strategies and ineffective methods standard medical care uses currently.

Next on the list may be family. Usually, when a family sticks with their injured member, they support them. And so, when brain injury requires conscious effort for every daily activity, it’s disingenuous to ask you to put family (or friends) ahead of yourself. While a non-injured person can look after their basic needs, and so have the bandwidth to support others, people with brain injury struggle to look after their own basic needs, from remembering to brush their teeth to making a proper meal as opposed to grabbing a chocolate bar when extreme hunger reminds them too late.

Elevating family above health leads to worsening neuro-fatigue and having no chance at meeting your own goals, no matter how modest. When I’ve placed family above my own goals or my own health, I have always suffered and set back my progress. After too many years of this, I learnt my lesson and placed my goals and my health above my family’s desires. When family doesn't recognize the catastrophe of your brain injury, trying to make them happy doesn’t change a thing other than worsening your health. But when I stuck to keeping health as my topmost priority over family, my self-esteem rose through meeting my own goals, and my health improved. Same with friends.

When priorities clash, I use the decision-tree method.

“Draw a vertical line down the middle of the page and at the top of the page, title each column with decision options. For example, I created a decision tree to decide whether or not to travel to England. I titled the columns ‘Visit England’ and ‘Don’t Visit England.’ Draw two vertical lines down the page, one underneath each option. Write ‘Pros’ and ‘Cons’ at the top of the columns for each option. Now list supportive points in each column without thinking. For example, the pros and cons of visiting England, and the pros and cons of not visiting England. When done, you’ll notice what stands out. Discuss with your therapist or trusted person if you’re still unsure. For me, the biggest con was financial. I asked myself if financial cost overrode the biggest benefit. It didn’t, and I found a way to afford it. As a result, I experienced benefits that paid off dramatically in non-financial ways, and the money resolved itself in the end.” Chapter 26, Brain Injury, Trauma, and Grief: How to Heal When You Are Alone.

Read more about decision-making in my book.

Bottom line: decide on your topmost priority. Keep that at the top of all top-priority lists unless you realize it’s not as important to you as you’d thought. Use methods like the decision tree. Learn financial literacy if you can. Putting health topmost improves functionality and makes choosing a priority easier.

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: For Better and Worse: Talking About the Future of Marriage
item.description:
Gender

For Better and Worse: Talking About the Future of Marriage

Stephanie Coontz's new book reminds us why and how gender matters.

Posted June 24, 2026

Key points
  • Gender segregation in work is higher in egalitarian societies than in misogynist ones.
  • Separate spheres ideology from industrialization still shapes gender roles and marriages today.
  • Overcoming unconscious biases requires recognizing the legacy of separate gender spheres.
For Better and Worse
Source: Stephanie Coontz / Viking Publishers, 2026

If you read one book this year about the state of marriage today, make it Stephanie Coontz’s new one, For Better and Worse (Viking, 2026).

It is an engaging romp through the history of human mating, from stone age marriage to the contradictory consequences of democracy for heterosexual coupling, to the possibilities of creating satisfying marriages in today’s heteropessimistic world. Rather than provide you with a summary of this monograph, I’m going to suggest you actually read it. Your investment of time will be well rewarded with the delight of enjoying a well-told, important, and historically accurate story.

In this blog, where I write about Gender Questions, I want to highlight just how well Professor Coontz shows us that gender, indeed, has always mattered, and still continues to do so today. Despite having read all of Coontz’s earlier books, there were totally new gems of knowledge in this one that helped me to better understand gender inequality. I want to share one of them with you here.

Gender Segregation in Egalitarian vs. Misogynist Societies

I have always been challenged by a paradox in contemporary research about gender inequality: gender segregation in the labor force is more exaggerated in egalitarian societies than in far more misogynistic societies. For example, Coontz writes that the World Economic Forum’s Global Gender Gap Index shows that when societies have more gender equal laws and social programs, women are less likely to enter male-dominated, higher-paying STEM occupations than in less egalitarian societies. Why would Saudi Arabia have more women scientists than Denmark?

The answer often offered by social scientists depends upon biological essentialism, the belief that women and men are just naturally different. In poor societies, women ignore their preferences for economic security. Less gender-egalitarian societies are often lower income, with few safety nets. In such societies, women need to enter the highest-paying jobs possible to attain economic security for themselves and their families. In more egalitarian societies, particularly the Nordic countries, safety nets exist. Women have more free choice of occupations, and so can indulge their passions, their supposedly inherent interests in people rather than things. In societies where their preferences matter, they choose careers that require caretaking and nurturing skills. With fewer severe economic constraints, this argument goes, women ‘s “true” nature can assert itself, and they choose to be teachers, nurses, and social workers, rather than engineers and scientists, money and prestige be damned.

What historian Coontz teaches us is that there is not actually any universal “feminine” set of interests or aptitudes. Men and women in more misogynistic societies actually have smaller differences in their self-reported personalities, capabilities, and preferences than those in more egalitarian and democratic societies. How can this be? As always, Coontz turns to a nuanced view of history to help explain this paradox.

The Impact of Industrialization and Separate Spheres on Gender Roles

As Western societies industrialized, and economic work left the household and morphed into paid labor in factories and offices, the ideology of separate spheres reared its very gendered head. The economic world became competitive, heartless, and understood to be masculine. Women were left, as Christopher Lasch wrote, to be the center of the family, which became a “haven in a heartless world.” The public sphere, which required rational and efficient skills, became masculine. The private sphere that was the province of wives and mothers became the site for warmth, caring, and emotional labor. Men came to be defined as the people with the skills required for analytic thinking, including science, technology, and math. Women came to be seen as the people with the skills required for caretaking, nurturing, and managing people. Before this time, men were involved in their families and caretaking, and women shared responsibilities for the household's economic labor. But with separate spheres came the belief in two different kinds of human beings, men and women. The sexes came to be seen as complementary opposites.

And such beliefs are not external to our own psyches! There is a great deal of experimental research that shows that when you make gender salient, women in Western societies act more feminine, and men more masculine. And when you remove gender stereotypes from the equation, such differences diminish markedly. For example, Coontz presents evidence from an intriguing experiment in which people were randomly assigned a male or female online avatar in a virtual reality game. They then entered a math game competition, with opposite-gender avatars. Participants with male avatars competing against female avatars consistently performed better than those assigned a female avatar. What is even more persuasive is that men who were assigned a female avatar performed worse. They lived down to the feminine, not-good-at-math stereotype.

The Unconscious Bias of Separate Spheres in Modern Life

Those of us who live in more egalitarian societies carry the unconscious bias of the separate sphere ideology with us into every moment of our lives, including our career choices. Those from more misogynist societies may have many more gendered struggles than we have, but not the legacy of the Western separate sphere ideology of the early phases of the industrial revolution.

And why does this all matter for marriage? Because those of us in post-industrial democratic Western societies continue to carry the legacy of the separate spheres in our psyches and therefore into our marriages as well. Even when husbands and wives work for pay full-time and want to equally share the family labor, those old stereotypes often trip us up.

Should you want some tips for how to move forward, to overcome such unconscious biases in your own marriage, let me recommend the last chapter of For Better and Worse by Stephanie Coontz. But do finish the rest of her book first. It’s a great summer beach read. Enjoy!

item.title: Helping Children and Teens Manage Anxiety
item.description:
Adolescence

Helping Children and Teens Manage Anxiety

We can identify the source of a kid's anxiety and manage it.

Posted June 24, 2026

Key points
  • Naming the "lion" reduces its power.
  • Regulation, not elimination, is the goal.
  • Understand the anxieties and how to name them.

There was a time when human survival depended on responding quickly to real danger. If a lion appeared, the body reacted instantly with a racing heart, tightening muscles, breathing quickly, and getting ready to pounce or run.

Today, children, adolescents, and young adults aren’t facing actual lions, but they are having the same physiological response of arousal, hypervigilance, and constant alertness. The brain continues to detect “threats,” even when those threats are psychological, social, or anticipatory. Events such as an upcoming test, a social interaction, a text message from a peer, or not fitting in can create the same physiological responses, nonetheless.

Let’s call the sources of anxiety for our children, teens, and young adults the “perceived lion.” The goal is not to eliminate anxiety, but to help children and teens recognize, interpret, and respond to it in more adaptive ways. A perceived lion is any situation the brain interprets as threatening, even when there is no actual physical danger. The brain does not always distinguish between real danger and anticipated or imagined threat.

For a child, the lion might be walking into school or separating from a parent. For a teenager, it may be a social event, a test, or a social gathering. For a young adult, it might involve fear of failure, rejection, or not meeting expectations.

Step One: Help the Young Person Name the Lion

One of the most effective starting points is helping the child or teen identify what, specifically, their brain is reacting to.

Instead of asking, “What’s wrong?” try:

  • “What feels like the lion right now?”
  • “What is your brain telling you might happen?”
  • “What are you most afraid of right now?”

As a parent, you can say:

  • It sounds like your lion right now is speaking in front of a group.
  • It sounds like your lion right now is having a difficult conversation.

When anxiety is externalized and named, it becomes less overwhelming. It shifts from an undefined sense of dread to something that can be observed, discussed, and worked with. This naming process alone often reduces intensity by creating psychological distance between the person and the fear.

Step Two: Assess the Actual Level of Danger

Once the perceived lion is identified, the next step is helping the young person differentiate between perceived threat and actual risk.

Ask:

  • “Is there a real danger to your safety right now?”
  • “What is the worst realistic outcome here?”
  • “If the worst happened, how would you deal with it?”

The intention is not to dismiss the anxiety or minimize emotional discomfort, but to help re-engage the logical parts of our brain. Anxiety focuses on threat, and asking these questions helps to shift your child’s mindset from emergency to worry or fear, which is much more manageable.

Step Three: Ground, Regulate, Co-Regulate

Even when insight is present, the body often remains activated. This is why physiological regulation is essential.

We can support our children and teens through co-regulation, such as taking deep breaths together, physically hugging or holding hands, and taking deep breaths, physical movement such as walking or even tapping. The goal is to take the nervous system out of panic mode and to feel in control again.

Over time, repeated experiences—“I can calm my body and get through this”—build internal confidence and resilience. We can then teach our kids that the experience of anxiety will peak and fall, and that we are capable of moving through it successfully.

Ultimately, anxiety management in children and teens is not about removing all “lions.” It is about helping them recognize a true threat, rather than a fear of rejection or failure. Instead, our goal is to equip them with the tools to respond and manage successfully.

When we support our kids and teens in naming their fear, evaluating its accuracy, and regulating their physiological response, they are not simply reducing anxiety in the moment. Instead, we are teaching them how to manage big emotions and fears in a way that builds confidence and resilience.

item.title: The Daily Choice That Keeps Relationships Alive
item.description:
Relationships

The Daily Choice That Keeps Relationships Alive

New research on how commitment builds bonds and betrayal breaks them.

Posted June 24, 2026

Key points
  • Commitment builds through small, consistent actions over time, but betrayal can undo that work in a moment.
  • Commitment shows up in five ways: fidelity, prioritization, investment, wholeheartedness, and endurance.
  • Betrayal goes beyond infidelity and includes lying, aggression, and unequal commitment.

With co-author D. Scott Sibley, Ph.D.

In a family therapy session that I (Jason) facilitated, Jeff was getting frustrated at his wife, Joni (names and details have been changed). “I know what I did was wrong,” he told her, his voice rising, and his finger pointing at her face. “But I have been working really hard to make it up to you, and you need to be accountable and do your part!”

Joni became visibly upset. “You hurt me!” she said. “You lost your temper, lashed out with insults, threw the remote, and pushed me in front of the children.”

Jeff was annoyed and thought the issue had been discussed to death. “I am sorry, and I haven’t done anything like that for a year," he pointed out. "I feel like I’m doing all the work, and you can’t get past it. Can’t we just move on?”

Source: Pixabay

When Betrayal Damages the Bond

Intimate relationships are a system, and all parties contribute to them. But as I explained to Jeff in that therapy session, betrayals are a shock to that system. When one person damages the other, the connection often needs intensive care and time to heal. This marriage had been rocked because Joni’s trust in Jeff and her sense of safety had been harmed. Since the verbal and physical aggression, every time Jeff escalated in tone or defensiveness, it scared Joni and aggravated her emotional wounds.

I explained to Jeff that when he got impatient with Joni and demanded she trust him, it was like yelling at a flower to regrow after it has been stepped on. Not only is it impossible, but it adds another injury to the delicate recovery process. If he wanted to get to a healthier place in his relationship, he needed to focus on consistent and caring commitment with his wife.

Commitment Builds Slowly, Betrayal Disrupts Quickly

Jeff and Joni’s experience reflect findings from recent research I have been conducting on healthy and unhealthy intimate relationships. Working with master’s student Megan Van Alfen, we examined how couples experience commitment and betrayal. We analyzed more than 80 in‑depth interviews with individuals who described experiences from their most meaningful connection to their most painful harms. Across interviews, commitment was consistently described as essential to relational bonds, while betrayals were described as damaging.

One of the key findings from this project was that commitment is often experienced as a gradual buildup of actions over time, like spending quality and quantity time with each other, and being loyal. On the opposite end of the spectrum were interactions described as betrayals, including infidelity, lying, or aggression, like what happened between Jeff and Joni. Betrayals were usually discrete events, and they damaged the growth created from sustained commitment.

Enduring Love Requires Active Protection

What we found aligns with decades of relationship scholarship showing that enduring love does not automatically flourish but must be actively nurtured and protected. Healthy relationships require effort and prioritization, along with restraint from damaging behaviors. Across many studies, perceived partner commitment is one of the strongest predictors of relationship quality, satisfaction, and long‑term stability. Commitment fosters a sense of security that helps couples to weather the inevitable bumps and conflict that come when two lives become one.

Protecting a relationship does not mean avoiding conflict altogether but developing patterns of interaction that prevent relational injury. Couples who fare best handle their differences with respect and patience. Flourishing couples repair missteps and resist impulses that trade short‑term bluntness for long‑term trust. When commitment functions this way, it allows partners to face challenges together rather than turning against one another.

5 Everyday Acts of Commitment

In our interviews, couples described everyday acts of commitment as a relational buffer, made of choices that helped them handle stress as a team rather than adversaries. They did not describe commitment as a vague feeling or promise, but as a pattern of action expressed across five interrelated dimensions: 1) fidelity, 2) prioritization, 3) relational investment, 4) whole‑heartedness, and 5) endurance.

Commitment can be understood as a conscious, active decision to be dedicated to one’s partner expressed through words and actions. As one of the participants said: "We know that we’re there for each other. We know that there’s not anything that is going to tear us apart, that’s going to separate us from the marriage, the love that we have."

Betrayal Beyond Infidelity

Betrayal, by contrast, refers to actions that violate the integrity and expectations in intimate relationships. Participants identified several forms of betrayal, including 1) turning to someone or something outside of the relationship, such as affairs or addictions; 2) lying or deception; 3) unequal levels of commitment; and 4) aggression. While these behaviors varied in severity, they were always destabilizing.

What made these experiences feel like betrayals was not only what happened, but what was lost. Participants lost confidence in their partners and fractured the moral core of the relationship itself. When people are disloyal, dishonest, or cruel, they undermine their foundation. One participant summarized this experience: “He never hurt me physically. But he hurt my heart over and over and over again.”

Small Efforts Make a Big Difference

So, what does this mean for couples?

We live in a world that demands our time and attention, often leaving little energy for what matters most. Most people say their intimate relationships are their highest priorities, yet as life pulls them in multiple directions, those relationships can wither and break. The good news is that even small efforts matter. As our research shows, commitment builds safety and connection, and this is an ongoing decision and investment. With patience and care, a loving relationship can heal and thrive through commitment.
